<!-- The answer key of the orientation's regression quiz: for each question of questions.md, the expected decision with its path and scope qualifications, the wrong answers to watch for, where the skill gives the rule, and its evidence in the record as of 2026-10-22, with cases 10, 12, 18, 21 and 22 read again on 2026-10-23, cases 5, 7, 21 and 23 on 2026-10-24, case 10 on 2026-10-30, cases 24 and 25 added on 2026-10-31, case 21 read again on 2026-11-06, cases 5, 12, 16 and 21 read again and cases 26 to 29 added on 2026-11-07, and cases 6, 16 and 17 read again and case 30 added on 2026-11-08, and cases 5, 16, 22, 26, 28 and 29 read again and case 31 added on 2026-11-09; for the grader only, never for the reader. -->

# Regression quiz: the key

## How to use it

The reader answers `questions.md` with only `CLAUDE.md`, the `fortress-repo` skill's core, its area parts and the orientation. The grader compares each answer with its case below (`../quiz-grade.md`): **right**, **wrong**, or **right without its path or scope qualification**. Grade the decision and its scope, not the wording, and not whether the reader names the record entries. An answer that says "look it up first" is right only if it also says where, and what it does with each result the key names.

Each case gives:

- **Trap**: the default assumption that the case tests, and where it is on record: the pretraining quiz (`explorations/reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md`, "the quiz"), its audit (`explorations/reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md`, "the audit"), or a worker's failure.
- **Expected**: the decision. **Scope**: the path and switch-over qualifications that a full answer needs.
- **Wrong**: answers that fail the case. **Partial**: what counts as right without its qualification.
- **Skill**: where a reader of the skill finds the rule: the core (`SKILL.md`), an area part (`references/X.md`), or the orientation (by the subject of its rule, since the orientation's text changes). A failed case counts against the orientation only if one of its passages misled the reader, or a rule that the case needs is in none of these places (`../quiz-grade.md`).
- **Evidence**: the record's entries (FACTS `F-N`, POSITIONS `P-N`, gap-ledger rows), read on `main` at `b9090d9bd` (2026-10-22). Climb batch 21's update read cases 10, 12, 18, 21 and 22 again on `main` at `66ed71f52` (2026-10-23), after its findings on the self type in the exclusion test (P-157) and on `Index` (P-156). Climb batch 21b's update read cases 5, 7 and 21 again and added case 23 on `main` at `aff478ca5` (2026-10-24), after its finding that `/` on two integers answers a `QQ` (F-284, the admission's change A) and the closing of row 584 (`108ab82d6`). After climb batch 22c, case 10 was read again on `main` at `79e5202ad` (2026-10-30): its rung B gives an unbounded type parameter the bound `Any` on `fortress compile` too (F-296) and closes row 412 (`1bc0a9083`). Climb batch 24's update added cases 24 and 25 on `main` at `453898c32` (2026-10-31), after its rung G made the code generator compile a declaration's own `where` clause (F-181; rows 701 and 867), and F-270 measured that a compiled call that opens a value of a trait of `NatParam`'s shape fails verification (row 307). Climb batch 26's update read case 21 again on `main` at `d7a03f34f` (2026-11-06), after its rung W made walk load a program's own vector-scalar pairs (F-318; row 804, fixed `c41c3d2b0`). Climb batch 27's update read cases 5, 12, 16 and 21 again and added cases 26 to 29 on `main` at `0549157f4` (2026-11-07), after its rung N opened and emptied `Number` (P-160, P-165, F-324; row 918), its rung E gave `SEQV` the specification's rule on both paths (P-168, F-326; row 923), and its rung A made walk print its numeral classes by the traits' names (P-167, F-328; row 364's new text) (climb batch 27's `orientation/admission.md`). Climb batch 28's update read cases 6, 16 and 17 again and added case 30 on `main` at `72bad2e25` (2026-11-08), after its rung on the integer conversions gave the five integer types the checked getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` and `asZZ`, which raise `IntegerOverflow`, kept `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` as the low-bits forms, and deleted `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` (P-161, F-331; row 349) (climb batch 28's `orientation/admission.md`). Its runs under walk and compiled, from a scratch folder and not kept, are quoted in those cases' **Evidence**. Climb batch 29's update read cases 5, 16, 22, 26, 28 and 29 again and added case 31 on `main` at `5febd82a78` (2026-11-09), after its rungs made a numeral convert where its place fixes a type and take its default elsewhere, on both paths (P-173, F-341, F-342, F-79; rows 454 and 944 closed), folded an expression of numerals alone exactly before the checker on both paths (F-339), made two string literals of one text one object and folded `||` of literals into one literal (F-343; rows 943 and 945 closed), and made walk read a number or string value at its trait where it infers a static argument (F-344; row 364 closed) (climb batch 29's `orientation/admission.md`). Its runs under walk, from a scratch folder and not kept, are quoted in those cases' **Evidence**.
- **Since the audit**: where the audit's answer of 2026-10-08 no longer holds.

The record does not fully settle ten cases: 2 (which way to record the defect), 18 (which repair) and, in one detail each, 21 (the reader's program spelled with the library's `+`), 22 (when the model program's own unbounded index parameters take the bound), 23 (what a compiled `/` on two integers does before the switch-over), 24 (whether the code generator is to refuse a `where`-clause variable at compile time), 25 (what `reflect` itself does compiled), 26 (whether a trait that promises a float is to bound such code), 27 (walk's refusal on a warm cache) and 29 (whether walk's instance at the class of another value, as `Ratio` for a `QQ`, is a departure). Each says so under **Open**.

----
## Case 5: a `long` into a `double`

- **Trap.** Java's implicit `long` to `double` widening, and with it the default that a float literal makes the quotient a float. Worker failures: the team demos `BiCGSTAB` and `BiCGSTAB2` divide a `ZZ64` by a float and stop under walk (row 791); the team demo `HeapShakedown` divides two `ZZ64`s, `(fin - start) / 10^6`, and gets a `Ratio` where an `RR64` is declared (row 449). Since climb batch 29 the float numeral no longer stops the line: it converts into `QQ` beside the `ZZ64`, and the quotient is an exact rational, the trap of row 174.
- **Expected.** Write the conversion: `seconds: RR64 = asFloat(elapsed) / 1000000000.0` (`1.0E9` too). A `ZZ64` goes into `RR64` only when written out, by `asFloat`, the explicit conversion that each number type declares in its own api (`ZZ64`'s at `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:633`; `Number` itself declares nothing, P-165, F-324), since the conversion can lose precision. Without it, the quotient is a rational, not a float. At a call, walk fits a numeral at its default and then by its own type's coercions (F-341): no `/` takes a `ZZ64` and an `RR64`, the float numeral converts into `QQ`, as `RadixPointNumeral` does (F-79), and the `ZZ64` coerces into `QQ`, so `QQ`'s `/` runs. `elapsed / 1000000000.0` is the exact `QQ` 3000000001/1000000000 for an `elapsed` of 3000000001. Untyped, `seconds = elapsed / 1000000000.0` is a rational, silently; `seconds: RR64 = elapsed / 1000000000.0` stops under walk at the binding: 'RHS expression type Ratio is not assignable to LHS type RR64'. `asFloat(elapsed / 1000000000)`, the exact rational converted once, is right too: it is the repair of row 449. If `elapsed` were a `ZZ32` (or a numeral), it would convert into `RR64` implicitly, so `elapsed / 1000000000.0` (3.0E-9 for a `ZZ32` 3) or `(1.0 elapsed) / 1000000000` would do.
- **Scope.** The rule is the interpreter's library's, which the compiled path reads after the switch-over. Until then the compiler's prelude differs (by reading, at `b9090d9bd`, and again at `aff478ca5`): its `RR64` coerces only from float literals and `RR32` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:434-435`), its `ZZ32` converts by a dotted `asRR64()`, its `ZZ64` declares no conversion into `RR64`, it has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64` (`:448`), and its `nanoTime()` answers an `RR64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi`). After the switch-over, by reading, the checker reads `elapsed / 1000000000.0` as walk does: no `/` takes a `ZZ64` with an `RR64` or a radix-point numeral, and both coerce into `QQ`, so `QQ`'s `/` is the one declaration that applies (F-342, F-79), and a typed `RR64` binding of it is refused statically. No record measures it. Not required for a right answer.
- **Wrong.** `elapsed / 1e9`, `elapsed / 1000000000.0`, or any implicit conversion, for the `ZZ64`: a `QQ`, not a float. `(1.0 elapsed) / 1.0E9`, the orientation's `(1.0 s) / n` form: it holds only for a `ZZ32` or a numeral, since `RR64` declares no coercion from `ZZ64` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:295-297` at `0549157f4`); `1.0 elapsed` converts the numeral into `QQ` beside the `ZZ64`, and the line answers the same exact `QQ`. `elapsed / 1000000000` with an integer divisor: `/` on two integers answers a `QQ`, not a float (F-284, row 449).
- **Partial.** The `asFloat` line, with no word on the `ZZ32` case. Keeping `asFloat` for a `ZZ32` is not wrong: each of the eight number types and the two numeral types declares its own (P-165; `ZZ32`'s at `FortressLibrary.fsi:564`). Where the reader says the conversion is declared does not change the grade.
- **Skill.** `library.md`, "The curator's decisions on the library" (the `RR64` bullet); core, "Numbers are siblings" (a wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one); the orientation's rule that `/` on two integers answers a `QQ` (its sentence "Convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`"), its rule that a numeral converts where it stands, and its rule that `Number` declares nothing, each type its own `asFloat`, in "Numbers". No passage of the skill states the rational that a float numeral makes beside a `ZZ64`: a reader who writes `asFloat` and expects the unconverted line to stop, 'Failed to find any matching overload' (this key's answer until climb batch 29), is right on the case; one who expects it to give a float is wrong.
- **Evidence.** P-74, F-131, F-284; P-165, F-324, F-311 (each type's own `asFloat`); rows 791 and 449, both fixed in `5e60e356a` by an `asFloat` in the demos (the failures stand as the trap's evidence); P-173, F-341, F-342, F-79, row 174 (the rational where a float is meant). Climb batch 29's update ran these under walk on `main` at `5febd82a78`, from a scratch folder, not kept: for `elapsed: ZZ64 = 3000000001`, `elapsed / 1000000000.0` and `(1.0 elapsed) / 1000000000.0` each printed '3000000001/1000000000', a `QQ`, and `seconds: RR64 = elapsed / 1000000000.0` stopped, 'RHS expression type Ratio is not assignable to LHS type RR64'; `asFloat(elapsed) / 1000000000.0` printed an `RR64` for an `elapsed` of 3000000000, '3.0'; for `e32: ZZ32 = 3`, `e32 / 1000000000.0` printed the `RR64` '3.0E-9'.
- **Since earlier keys.** Until climb batch 27 this key said that `asFloat` is the conversion that `Number` declares, as the library then did. Climb batch 27 struck it from `Number` (P-165, F-324); the expected line does not change. Until climb batch 29 it said that walk stops on `elapsed / 1000000000.0`, 'Failed to find any matching overload'; since walk fits a numeral by its own type's coercions (F-341), the line answers a `QQ`. The expected line does not change.

----
## Case 16: a numeral at an `NN32` binding

- **Trap.** Since climb batch 29 the default from Java, that a numeral binds to any integer type as a literal to `int`, is right, and the trap is the old answer, that walk refuses the binding. It is this key's answer until climb batch 29; the orientation's old rule, under walk a numeral is a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` "until walk runs the checker"; `tests-writing.md:34`, "Write `a: NN32 = unsigned(5)`, not `a: NN32 = 5`"; and the audit's A5, a numeral binds to `NN32` on neither path (`explorations/reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md:62`) (climb batch 29's `orientation/admission.md`, P-173's and F-341's rows). A second trap, for a test that checks the value: the three-argument `assert` taken to convert the numeral as the binding does.
- **Expected.** The binding works on both paths: `n: NN32 = 3` binds the `NN32` 3. A typed binding is a place that fixes a type, and the numeral converts there exactly from its value into `NN32` (P-173; F-341 under walk, F-342 compiled). Write it as it is. `unsigned(3)` and `(3).asNN32` give 3 too, but are not needed.
- **Scope.** Walk converts when the line runs and refuses there a numeral outside `NN32`'s range, as `n: NN32 = -1`; the checker refuses it statically (P-173). On the compiled path before the switch-over, the checker types the numeral as `IntLiteral`, the compiler's prelude's name for the numeral type, which `NN32` converts from (row 454's notes). The two conversions differ only at a value that does not fit: `unsigned` keeps the low bits, so at a negative value it wraps where `asNN32` raises `IntegerOverflow` (P-161). The getter needs the numeral in parentheses: `3.asNN32` is one malformed numeral to the parser, 'Syntax Error: a numeral contains letters and does not have a radix specifier' (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Literal.rats:87-99`). A test that checks the value writes `assert(n = 3, msg)`, or `assert(n, unsigned(3), msg)` as `tests/NumeralTypesWalk.fss:60` does. In `assert(n, 3, msg)` the numeral meets `assert`'s parameter of type `Any` and takes its default, a `ZZ32` (P-173), which no coercion joins to `NN32`, so the two compare by `SEQV` (P-165, F-324) and the assertion fails under walk, 'FAIL: a NN32: 3 =/= a ZZ32: 3'; `n =/= 3` is `true` in the same way (row 966). None of these points is needed for a right answer; a reader who names the assertion trap is right.
- **Wrong.** The binding refused under walk, with `unsigned(3)` or `(3).asNN32` given as the needed form; "refused on both paths"; the getter written `3.asNN32`, which does not parse.
- **Partial.** The binding said to work under walk, with no compiled answer, or the reverse.
- **Skill.** The orientation's rule "A numeral converts where it stands (P-173)", in "Numbers" (its example `u: NN32 = 5`), and its rule that an integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function. `tests-writing.md:34` still says that under walk a numeral does not bind to `NN32` (row 454, closed by `3de571bac7`), and `interpreter.md`'s list of walk's departures on literals (`:18-25`) is stale too (climb batch 29's `orientation/admission.md`, "Elsewhere"): a reader misled there fails the case against that area part, not against the orientation.
- **Evidence.** P-173, F-341, F-342, F-79, P-76; row 454 (`FIXED`, `3de571bac`); `tests/NumeralTypesWalk.fss:59-61` (`n: NN32 = 5`, asserted against `unsigned(5)` and of kind `NN32`) and `:77-84` (`u0 = 0` and `0 = u0` for an `NN32` zero); P-161, F-331 (`ZZ32`'s `asNN32` raises only below 0: `compile-ladder/rung-integer-conversions/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why", the getters' table; `tests/IntegerConversionsWalk.fss:74-75`); for the assertion, row 966 (`tests/XXXNotEqualNumeral.fss`) and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:96-98`, `:307-308` (`=` and `=/=` over `Any`, and `assert(x:Any, y:Any, ...)` testing `x =/= y`). Climb batch 29's update ran these under walk on `main` at `5febd82a78`, from a scratch folder, not kept: `n: NN32 = 3` printed 3, of type `NN32`; `n = 3` printed `true` and `n =/= 3` `true`; `assert(n, 3, "three")` failed, 'FAIL: a NN32: 3 =/= a ZZ32: 3; three'; `assert(n = 3, "three")` passed. Climb batch 28's runs of `(3).asNN32`, `unsigned(3)` (each 3, under walk and compiled) and `3.asNN32` (the parse error) stand.
- **Since the audit and earlier keys.** A5 says that a numeral binds to `NN32` on neither path; the compiled half was fixed first (row 454's notes), and walk's at climb batch 29. Until climb batch 29 this key's expected answer was that walk refuses the binding, 'RHS expression type Int is not assignable to LHS type NN32', and that `unsigned(3)` or `(3).asNN32` is needed there. That answer is now wrong.

## Case 26: numbers of two types compared, and a float from generic code over `Number`

- **Trap.** Two numbers of different types compare by value, as `1 == 1.0` does in Java, Scala and Julia; and any number converts to a float, as by Java's `Number.doubleValue()`. The team's 2012 library said the same: its `trait Number` declared an abstract `asFloat` and an `=` through it (`git show a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, lines 349-357), as the revival's library did until climb batch 27, and this key's case 5 with it. Since climb batch 29 a third default meets it: a numeral folds and converts, so `1/2 = 0.5` is `true` (P-173), and a reader can carry that to typed values of the two types. Worker failures: the revival's `tests/FlatTowerRungF.fss:75-76` (`assert(1/2 = 0.5, ...)`, `deny(big(3) = 3.5, ...)`) and the team's `testRR32.fss:67-75` and `expTest.fss:22`, `:24` leaned on the old `=` and were respelled with `asFloat`; two of the team's library bodies called `asFloat` on a `Number`, `Float`'s `^` and the `RR64` trait's `atan2`, which the checker refused, 'Could not check call to function asFloat', once `Number` was emptied (`compile-ladder/rung-number-open/REPORT.md`, "Each comparison respelled" and "The stages"). Neither quiz tests it (climb batch 27's `orientation/admission.md`, P-165's row).
- **Expected.**
  - (a) `asFloat(count) = limit`. `count = limit` gives `false` for 3 and 3.0, with no error: no coercion joins `ZZ64` and `RR64` (a `ZZ64` goes into `RR64` only written out, P-74), so the library declares no `=` between them, and `=` falls to its fallback `opr =(a:Any, b:Any) = a SEQV b` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:96`); values of different types are never strictly equivalent (P-168, F-326). For `count: ZZ32`, `count = limit` compares by value, `true` for 3 and 3.0, since `RR64` coerces from `ZZ32` and the library declares a pair of `=` for each of its 21 coercions (F-324); `asFloat(count) = limit` is right there too. For `count: QQ` no coercion joins `QQ` and `RR64`, so `count = limit` is `false` again, as `q = lim` is for `q: QQ = 1/2` and `lim: RR64 = 0.5`: write `asFloat(count) = limit`, as for the `ZZ64`. A numeral differs: `1/2 = 0.5`, numerals alone, folds exactly into `true` (P-173, F-339), and `q = 0.5` is `true` too, since the float numeral converts into `QQ` at `QQ`'s `=` (F-341). Only two typed values of the two types compare by `SEQV`.
  - (b) Not `asFloat(a)` over `T extends Number`: `Number` declares nothing (P-165, F-324), so the checker refuses the call, 'Could not check call to function asFloat', each type's `asFloat` being 'not applicable to an argument of type Number', and the count stage counts it. Declare `near` at `RR64`, `near(a: RR64, b: RR64): Boolean`: coercion carries a `ZZ32`, an `RR32` or a numeral into it at the call, and a `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ` or `QQ` argument is written `near(asFloat(x), b)` (F-323, the library's form for `random`, `atan2`, the `RR64` trait's `^` and `printThreadInfo`). Or declare it at each number type, each body by that type's own `asFloat`, as the library declares the vector norm (F-324). Either is right.
- **Scope.** (a) is the interpreter's library's rule, which both paths read after the switch-over; `SEQV` answers so on both paths (F-326). Until the switch-over the compiler's prelude declares no `asFloat` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:96`) and its `ZZ64` no conversion into `RR64` (case 5). (b) Walk checks no static types, so it would run the generic body for an argument whose type declares `asFloat`, which proves nothing (by reading; F-57 records the like case of `x + 1` in code generic over `Integral`, refused by the checker and run by walk). `NN32` does not convert into `RR64` yet (F-131, P-75). None of these points is needed for a right answer.
- **Wrong.** (a) `count = limit` as the condition, or said to give `true`; `(1.0 count) = limit` (case 5's wrong form: `RR64` declares no coercion from `ZZ64`, and `1.0 count` is a `QQ`); `count = limit` kept for the `QQ`, or said to be `true` there because `1/2 = 0.5` is. (b) `asFloat(a)` at `T extends Number`, taken as right because walk runs it; `asFloat` declared on `Number` again, or on a new trait that the number types extend, added to the library without a decision of the curator (P-165; **Open**).
- **Partial.** (a) The `asFloat` line right, with `count = limit` said to raise an error rather than answer `false`, or with no word on the `ZZ32` and `QQ` cases. (b) A declaration at `RR64` or at each type, with no word on why the generic one fails.
- **Open.** Whether such code is to take a bound that promises a float is fork N8 of climb batch 27, on the curator's review queue (`explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`, item 393: "a small trait with `asFloat` as the norm's bound"); its default is as landed, one declaration at each type. A reader who proposes such a trait as a decision not taken, and meanwhile declares (b) at `RR64` or at each type, is right. The `false` of a `ZZ64` against an `RR64` is by reading of the 42 pairs, none of which joins the two, and of the measured rule of `SEQV` across types (`tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss:19`, a `ZZ32` and an `RR64`); Appendix I states it (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2776-2782`).
- **Skill.** The orientation's rule that `Number` declares nothing, in "Numbers", its rules that a numeral converts where it stands and that numerals alone fold, and its rule that where a type declares no `=`, `=` is `SEQV`, in "Traits and objects"; `library.md`, "The curator's decisions on the library" (the `RR64` bullet, which names only `ZZ64` beside `ZZ32` and numerals); core, "Numbers are siblings".
- **Evidence.** P-165, P-160, P-74, P-168, F-324, F-323, F-326, F-131; for the numerals, P-173, F-339, F-341 (`tests/NumeralFoldWalk.fss`, `tests/NumeralTypesWalk.fss`). Climb batch 29's update ran these under walk on `main` at `5febd82a78`, from a scratch folder, not kept: `1/2 = 0.5` printed `true`; for `q: QQ = 1/2` and `lim: RR64 = 0.5`, `q = lim` printed `false` and `q = 0.5` `true`; for `l3: RR64 = 3.0`, a `ZZ64` 3 `= l3` printed `false` and a `ZZ32` 3 `= l3` `true`. Also `tests/NumberMixedEqualityWalk.fss:31-34` (a `ZZ32` 3 and an `RR64` 3.0 equal by the pair at `RR64`'s coercion), `tests/FlatTowerRungF.fss:75-76`, `tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss:17-20`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:295-297` (`RR64`'s three coercions) and `:321`, `:415`, `:502`, `:564`, `:633`, `:697` (the six traits' `asFloat`), at `0549157f4`; `compile-ladder/rung-number-open/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why", "The stages" and "Each comparison respelled"; climb batch 27's `orientation/admission.md`, P-165's row.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:105
- P-174 **A numeral's type exists only at compile time: the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, with its four numbers as static parameters; every number type, the library's too, takes a numeral through a coercion generic over the four numbers.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r` and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`), so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`; the four are naturals of any size, and read as values in a coercion's body they are exact integers, `ZZ`; this implementation's `NN32` bound (P-40) is for sizes. The coercion's body calls the type's constructor on values computed from the four numbers, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))`, and the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and folds it (P-176). No numeral value exists when a program runs: a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type, and is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. A numeral has no sign: at a program's type `-3` is the type's own prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result for `3`, and a type without `-` refuses it; any other expression of numerals alone folds first (P-173) and reaches such a type only through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`, since coercions do not chain. The design leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and `opr ||` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1662`). Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has libraries define the coercions into integers and rationals (`literals.tex:132-148`); the curator finishes that design, in place of the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). Rows 960 and 974 hold where the tree departs: the digit count of `00.5`, and walk running a numeral type written as a static argument or as a type that an object or a trait extends.

POSITIONS.md:104
- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:35
- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The one exception is the numerals: until the switch-over the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176, so that both paths treat a numeral alike before it, and that copy goes with the prelude. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:99
- P-165 **`asFloat` and the `=` built on it leave `trait Number`; each built-in number type keeps its own `asFloat`.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` each declare `asFloat`, so the written conversion `asFloat(x)` into `RR64` is unchanged at every concrete type; the numeral types declare none, since no numeral value exists when a program runs (P-174). Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other (P-74); otherwise the program writes the conversion, `asFloat(x) = y`. The vector norm takes a bound that promises a float; its form is the default of a fork on his review list: the norm at each of the eight number types, each by its own `asFloat` (F-324). `Float`'s `^` at a `Number` exponent, `random`, `atan2` and `printThreadInfo` are declared at `RR64`, and coercion carries `ZZ32`, `RR32` and numerals to them. The specification's sentence follows (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:58-75`). P-74's rule, an exact conversion implicit and a lossy one written, stands. Why: the team's compiler prelude declares `Number` with nothing in it (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:509`), and the specification does not ground the method: its sentence that names it on `Number` is the revival's revision. The curator's rule for such a case: an early idea of the interpreter's library goes where the specification does not ground it and the later prelude eliminated it. With `Number` open (P-160), an abstract `asFloat` would force a program's own number, such as a complex number, to invent a float, and `Number`'s `=` would compare two different complex numbers by it.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:38
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). The bound is this implementation's, for the sizes of arrays, vectors and matrices, to match the JVM's `int` indices; a numeral type's four static parameters have none, and read as values are `ZZ` (P-174). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array stops at its store's factory with walk's own error, which no catch sees (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:106
- P-176 **A numeral at a place denotes one value, the same on both paths and made once: the compiler folds the coercion instantiated for it (P-174), and walk runs that coercion at the place's first evaluation.** Where the result is a JVM `int`, `long`, `float` or `double`, the class file holds it as a constant; otherwise, as at `QQ` or a program's own type, the constructor call on the constants runs once per place, into a `static final` field filled when the class loads, and a program's type's own `-` on the numeral (P-174) runs there too. Walk fixes the coercion's static arguments from the numeral's four numbers and keeps the result for the place; it refuses a numeral only when the place runs, until it runs the checker (P-12). Before the switch-over the compiler's prelude carries this design (P-37), so that both paths give one value at one place. Why: a numeral is a constant of the program, and a JVM class file holds no object, so a field filled once at load is the nearest form of an object constant. Rows 957 and 971 hold where the tree departs: a place whose type names a type parameter, and a coercion that spawns a task.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics

FACTS.md:249
- F-346 **Under walk the library's `=` and `=/=` over `Any` meet a numeral at its default, so a number and a numeral of one value answer both as if the values differed.** Under walk `u = 0` is `false` and `u =/= 0` is `true` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, and so are `q = 0.5` and `q =/= 0.5` for `q: QQ = 1/2`: with no `=` pairs between a numeral type and a number type (P-174), `=` takes the numeral at its default (row 973), and `opr =/=(a:Any, b:Any) = NOT (a=b)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:98`) follows it (row 966). So under walk `e =/= e'` still answers `NOT (e = e')`. The compiled path until the switch-over answers `false` for `u =/= 0` through the prelude's `=/=` on each integer type. Test: `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXNotEqualNumeral.fss` (an expected failure), with `XXXNumeralEqualsNumberWalk.fss` for `u = 0`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-literals-spec/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why"; `compile-ladder/rung-static-numerals/REPORT.md`, "11. Defects, each with its home".

FACTS.md:247

# The orientation workflow

The `fortress-repo` skill's revival part, `references/revival-changes.md`, becomes the **orientation**: the short account of how revived Fortress departs from the original and from what a model expects, which every worker reads whole (Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`). `orientation.js` writes it, in two modes:

- **consolidate**, once, and again whenever the part has drifted: an outline by the concepts workers use and a table of where each old entry goes (`outline.md`); the writer writes the whole text from them; a preservation check against the table, a cold read with only the skill's core, and the regression quiz; the writer's fix round; a second cold read and the quiz again; a judge.
- **update**, after every landing: the landing's new and changed FACTS and POSITIONS entries pass the admission test (`admission.md`: the wrong default, the correction, the mistake it prevents); the writer rewrites the sections they touch in place, within the budget of 8K to 12K characters; the same checks, fix round, reread and judge.

The writer is a headless Opus stream (`../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`), so its fix round resumes the session that wrote the text. The regression quiz is kept in `regression/` (questions and key), and grows with each update.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/orientation.js',
               args: { mode: 'consolidate', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation', concepts: ['/abs/concepts.md'] } })
    Workflow({ scriptPath: ..., args: { mode: 'update', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation-bN', facts: ['F-261', 'P-153'] } })

## Installing its result

### A small test to preserve through consolidation

Keep the quiz and audit as historical evidence. Select a small set of consequential wrong assumptions from them and actual worker failures, then update the expected answers against the current record. The October 8 audit itself contains statements that later work may have changed; do not use its old answers as a timeless oracle.

For the whole-Revival consolidation, give a fresh reader the core skill, the proposed whole orientation and neutral task questions, without the audit or answer key. Grade concrete choices, including the path and scope qualifications, rather than its ability to repeat headings. For example: how to run a source program; what to do when the specification and an implementation disagree; and whether a numeric relationship or conversion assumed from another language holds here. Include a case where the right action is to follow a task-specific pointer or explore, not invent an answer.

The reviewer has the expected answers and evidence. Record missed corrections and new false assumptions. Compare old and new skill versions on the same cases when judging a consolidation regression. For later small edits, rerun only the affected cases; refresh the pretraining-only baseline when a materially different worker model makes that useful. This is a proposed bounded regression practice, not a claim that the earlier experiment already implemented it.

### Do named frameworks help?

ASD-STE100 is already named in the writer's standing brief and the writing principles, with concrete instructions about terminology, sentence structure and descriptive versus procedural text. The project uses an adaptation (“halfway”), not a demonstrated certification of compliance.

The useful ideas from the other responses should likewise become observable checks: introduce required concepts before relying on them; supply context at entry points; preserve a claim's conditions and evidence; and test whether a reader can make the intended decision. Much of this is already in the writing principles and cold reads.

Do not add Knowledge Space Theory, RST, GSN or other labels to the mandatory writer brief merely to sound more grounded. This review has not verified the external responses' descriptions of those frameworks, and no recommendation depends on those descriptions. If a framework later supplies a useful technique, record its source and the particular check it motivates in maintenance material. Naming a framework is not a substitute for specifying the reader failure to prevent.

## Recovered admission rule, workflow runs and transcript search pointers

Follow-up on October 22: the curator clarified that each Revival entry must earn its place by correcting a worker's default mental model to match **revived Fortress**. This is an admission test for each addition or edit, and a retention test during consolidation, not merely a final readability check.

### The original rule is on record

`explorations/reviews/skills-review-style.md`, Lens 10, gives the test verbatim:

> Test: name an agent that acts differently without the sentence. Name the record or transcript that shows the failure. If there is neither, cut it.

The same review records the curator's October 8 goal: use the agents' pretraining knowledge to guide them toward a correct mental model of Fortress. Section 2, M3 links that goal to the pretraining quiz and distillation audit. M4 records the October 5 05:54 request for a fresh reader and scenarios containing traps; it says this became cold reads given only the skill, followed by fixes and work on triggering/routing. Those times are as recorded in the artifact; their timezone was not independently verified.

This is stronger recovered support than the general “flag gotchas” instruction alone. The writer should require a default assumption, the correction for revived Fortress, and the consequential mistake avoided. Keep supporting evidence in sources or the evaluation record, not as another compulsory three-part paragraph in Revival.

### Actual automated work, distinguished from the unverified paired test

| Artifact | What it establishes |
|---|---|
| `explorations/reviews/fortress-repo-rewrite-points.md`, opening | A completed rewrite Workflow run, **`wf_185878c8-0fb`**, on October 8: sixteen writers, one per part, then three cold readers and fixes. Commits: `24af7743b` rewrite, `9a9c30d95` cold-read fixes, `cae2a0ad5` comparison. |
| `explorations/reviews/skills-description-optimization.md` | Executed skill-creator scripts on October 4, 20:05–20:40 UTC: 20 trigger/near-miss queries per skill, repeated runs, training/test split and description optimization. Fortress triggering improved from 52/60 to 59/60 runs. “Before/after” here means description versions, not worker answers without/with the skill. The evaluation files were outside git in `scratchpad/skills-description-optimization/`. |
| `explorations/reviews/skills-review-style.md`, M4 | Scenario/trap cold-reading was requested and performed according to the historical review. It does not give a paired no-skill/with-skill scoring protocol. |
| `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/skill-effect.md` | A comparison of actual earlier and later batch behaviour, not a controlled per-entry admission experiment. Concurrent workflow changes limit attribution to the skill. |

The October 4 held note also records an initial trigger/routing experiment that the curator stopped and replaced with the skill-creator's normal description optimization. See `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md` at `9e17a6937` (19:55:58 UTC) and `8806c5360` (20:03:36 UTC). The planned `skills-trigger-test.md` must not be cited as a completed result.

The evidence therefore confirms real automated evaluation and a real rewrite Workflow. It does **not yet verify** that the specific paired mental-model test remembered by the curator ran as a workflow. Do not conflate these procedures or conclude it never ran.

### Precise breadcrumbs for Claude's transcript search

The relevant commits carry Claude session **`session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB`**. Start in that session's history with:

- October 4, 19:55–20:40 UTC: initial testing worker, its cancellation, then skill-creator optimization.
- October 5, 05:54 as recorded in the style review: request for scenarios containing traps, then cold-reader launches.
- October 8: pretraining quiz, distillation audit, and Workflow **`wf_185878c8-0fb`**. Resolve its full ID in the workflow journal; the report preserves only this prefix.
- Search phrases: “scenarios that contain traps”, “name an agent that acts differently”, and the workflow ID.

Remote branches `transcripts` and `transcripts-blinded` were confirmed to exist. Their contents were not downloaded for this bounded review. Thus these are session, time and run pointers recovered from repository artifacts, **not an independently verified JSONL path or message ID**. Claude should inspect the actual launch briefs and results before claiming to have recovered the exact paired protocol.

### Operationalize the admission test, not another writing ritual

For consolidation, apply the admission test to each candidate correction. For later landings, apply it to each proposed addition or substantive edit. An established trap can reuse its evidence; do not rerun a baseline merely to satisfy a form. When necessity is uncertain, use a fresh-reader test.

A small Claude Workflow could separate three jobs: a scenario author establishes the expected decision and its evidence; fresh readers answer neutral matched scenarios with and without the candidate correction; a grader compares answers against the evidence. For an incremental edit, the baseline should normally be the existing skill **without the candidate**, not an entirely unassisted worker. Otherwise the test cannot show that this particular addition is needed. A no-skill baseline remains useful for discovering broader pretraining assumptions.

The scenario author and grader may see the record; test readers must not see the expected answers or each other's responses. Require correct decisions and scope, not recitation. A candidate earns space when it addresses an evidenced wrong assumption or consequential missing knowledge; if the baseline already handles the case, seek evidence from other relevant failures before retaining it. One passing answer is not proof that every future worker will know it.

This is a workflow outline for Claude to reconcile with the recovered run, not a claim about how that run was implemented. Keep the writer's instruction small: **identify the mistaken assumption, show why it is expected, and verify that the correction prevents the mistake without introducing another.** Preserve evaluation evidence in maintenance records. No skill files or workflow code were changed in this review.

## P45: fidelity and comprehensibility are separate checks

On October 22 the curator supplied a screenshot and copied text of a proposed P-45 revision from the positions audit. The artifact URL could not be retrieved; this review concerns the supplied example, not the entire list. The screenshot distinguishes deletions from retained text; the copied text alone mixes both. The original ruling and its provenance have not been re-audited here.

**Finding:** removing historical material improves the entry but does not by itself make the remaining decision understandable. The difficulty is visible in the formulation, not necessarily a lack of Fortress knowledge on the reader's part.

- It mixes requirements with statements of implementation behaviour. “The checker runs” and “walk and the checker accept the same pairs” read as established facts, while “Still to build” points to remaining disagreements. State clearly whether agreement is a requirement or an achieved result.
- “No parameter pair required to exclude”, “refused families” and “reads otherwise” conceal important meaning in compressed technical wording. Name the objects and the operation precisely.
- “The paper's three overloading rules” neither identifies the paper precisely nor states enough of the decision to orient the reader. A reference may supply detail; it should not replace the explanation of what was decided.
- “No model line changes” compresses a consequential constraint into project shorthand. Identify the microGPT model program and state the exact restriction established by the ruling.
- A tracked diff makes historical and current wording compete for attention. Show the clean proposed entry first, with the diff available underneath.

FACTS.md:76
- F-79 **In the interpreter's library, the numeral types are `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` and `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]`, traits whose static parameters are the four numbers, below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`, and each number type converts from them by a coercion generic over the four numbers.** It builds P-174's numeral types in the one library (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:457-465`): `NaturalNumeral` lies below `AnyNaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` below `AnyRadixPointNumeral`, which exclude each other; none declares a method, no value of them exists when a program runs, and no `=` pair ties them to a number type. The five integer types and `QQ` convert from `NaturalNumeral` exactly, `QQ` from `RadixPointNumeral` exactly, and `RR64` and `RR32` from both by one rounding through `simpleDoubleArith.numeralToDouble` and `numeralToFloat`; `RR64` comprises `Float` alone. The compiled checker's `Types.INT_LITERAL` and `FLOAT_LITERAL` name these two types under both libraries (`compiler/Types.java:85-95`), the prelude declaring them too. FACTS.md:161
- F-342 **The compiled checker converts a numeral where nothing fixes a type into its default, refuses one out of range, and refuses a numeral type written other than as a parameter's type.** Where no place's type has a coercion from the numeral's type (an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter, a receiver, a join, a result with no declared return type), a numeral becomes a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, or an `RR64` with a radix point. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default holding them all, and the conversion into the default ranks as no coercion. A numeral outside a bounded number type's range, or rounding to an infinity, is a static error, also as a tuple's element at a tuple type and in a result position of an `if`, a `case`, a `do` block or a `try`; a program's type with no coercion from the numeral's type refuses a numeral. `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` are written in a program only as a parameter's type, never as a type that an object or a trait extends. component NumeralOwnTypeWalk
export Executable

oneRounding(v: ZZ, r: ZZ32, m: ZZ32): RR64 =
    builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleDoubleArith.numeralToDouble")

value object CC64(re: RR64, im: RR64)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = CC64(oneRounding(v, r.asZZ32, 0), 0.0)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) =

    opr +(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re + other.re, im + other.im)
    opr juxtaposition(self, other: CC64): CC64 =
        CC64(re other.re - im other.im, re other.im + im other.re)
end

i: CC64 = CC64(0.0, 1.0)

exact(d: RR64): QQ = do
    bits: ZZ64 = d.rawBits
    e: ZZ64 = (bits RSHIFT 52) BITAND 2047
    f: ZZ64 = bits BITAND 4503599627370495
    mant: ZZ = big(f + 4503599627370496)
    k: ZZ32 = (e - 1075).asZZ32
    two: ZZ = big(2)
    if k >= 0 then (mant two^k) / big(1) else mant / two^(-k) end
  end

value object Iv(lo: RR64, hi: RR64)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = do
        q: QQ = v / r^(m.asZZ32)
        d: RR64 = oneRounding(v, r.asZZ32, m.asZZ32)
        a: QQ = exact(d)
        if a = q then Iv(d, d) elif q < a then Iv(d.nextDown, d) else Iv(d, d.nextUp) end
      end
end

value object BF16(bits: ZZ32)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = do
        q: QQ = v / r^(m.asZZ32)
        half: QQ = 1/2
        s: QQ = q (128/1)
        k0: ZZ = floor(s)
        rest: QQ = s - (k0/1)
        up: Boolean = if rest > half then true elif rest < half then false else odd(k0) end
        k: ZZ = if up then k0 + 1 else k0 end
        BF16((k - 128 + 16256).asZZ32)
      end
end

value object Dec(unscaled: ZZ, scale: ZZ32)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Dec(v, m.asZZ32)
end

digitsOf(v: ZZ, r: ZZ, n: ZZ32): String = do
    var s: String := ""
    var k: ZZ := v
    var j: ZZ32 := 0
    while k > big(0) OR j < n do
        d: ZZ32 = (k MOD r).asZZ32
        s := "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"[d] || s
        k := k DIV r
        j += 1
    end
    s
  end

suffix(r: ZZ): String = if r = big(10) then "" else "_" || r.asString end

value object RoundtripNumeral(text: String)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = do
        t = digitsOf(v, r, n.asZZ32)
        w = (n - m).asZZ32
        RoundtripNumeral(t[0#w] || "." || t[w#(m.asZZ32)] || suffix(r))
      end
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) =
        RoundtripNumeral(digitsOf(v, r, n.asZZ32) || suffix(r))
    getter asString(): String = text
end

writtenBack(w: RoundtripNumeral, s: String): () = assert(w.asString, s, "written back as " || s)
writtenBack(w: RoundtripNumeral, s: String, why: String): () = assert(w.asString, s, why)

object Ref(v: ZZ)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = Ref(v)
end

    assert(exact(piv.lo) < piq AND piq < exact(piv.hi), "Iv(3.1415926535897932384) encloses the numeral's exact value")
    assert(piv.lo.nextUp SEQV piv.hi, "Iv(3.1415926535897932384) is one ulp wide")

(* The static numerals compiled: a program's types take a numeral through coercions generic over its four numbers, a negative constant through the type's own minus, one value per place, and the defaults. *)
component NumeralStaticDesignCompiled
export Executable

tName(a: Any): String = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.typeName")
sEq(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.equality.sEquiv")
oneRounding(v: ZZ, r: ZZ32, m: ZZ32): RR64 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleDoubleArith.numeralToDouble")
small(z: ZZ): ZZ32 = bigToZZ64(z).asZZ32

value object CC64(re: RR64, im: RR64)
  coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = CC64(oneRounding(v, small(r), 0), 0.0)
  coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = CC64(oneRounding(v, small(r), small(m)), 0.0)
  opr -(self): CC64 = CC64(-re, -im)
  opr +(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re + other.re, im + other.im)
  opr -(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re - other.re, im - other.im)
  opr juxtaposition(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re other.re - im other.im, re other.im + im other.re)
end

i: CC64 = CC64(0.0, 1.0)

value object Dec(unscaled: ZZ, scale: ZZ32)
  coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Dec(v, small(m))
end

powZZ(b: ZZ, e: ZZ32): ZZ = if e = 0 then 1 else b powZZ(b, e - 1) end

value object BF16(bits: ZZ32)
  coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = do
    den: ZZ = powZZ(r, small(m))
    s: ZZ = v 128
    k0: ZZ = s DIV den
    rest: ZZ = s - k0 den
    twice: ZZ = rest + rest
    half: ZZ32 = small(k0) DIV 2
    up: Boolean = if twice > den then true elif twice < den then false else NOT (half + half = small(k0)) end
    k: ZZ32 = if up then small(k0) + 1 else small(k0) end
    BF16(k - 128 + 16256)
  end
end

hexDigit(d: ZZ32): String = "0123456789ABCDEF".substring(d, d + 1)
digitsOf(v: ZZ, r: ZZ, n: ZZ32): String = if n = 0 then "" else do front: String = digitsOf(v DIV r, r, n - 1); last: String = hexDigit(small(v - (v DIV r) r)); front || last end end
suffix(r: ZZ32): String = if r = 10 then "" else "_" || r.asString end

value object RoundtripNumeral(text: String)
  coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = do
    sn: ZZ32 = small(n)
    sm: ZZ32 = small(m)
    t: String = digitsOf(v, r, sn)
    w: ZZ32 = sn - sm
    sfx: String = suffix(small(r))
    RoundtripNumeral(t.substring(0, w) || "." || t.substring(w, sn) || sfx)
  end
  coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = do
    sn: ZZ32 = small(n)
    t: String = digitsOf(v, r, sn)
    sfx: String = suffix(small(r))
    RoundtripNumeral(t || sfx)
  end
  getter asString(): String = text
end

writtenBack(w: RoundtripNumeral, s: String): () = assert(w.asString, s, "written back as " || s)
writtenBack(w: RoundtripNumeral, s: String, why: String): () = assert(w.asString, s, why)

value object Tally(k: ZZ32, seen: ZZ, negated: Boolean)
  coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = Tally(small(v), v, false)
  opr -(self): Tally = Tally(-k, seen, true)
end

object Gen[\T\](v: ZZ32)
  coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = Gen[\T\](small(v))
end

site(): Gen[\RR64\] = 3

value object Byte(b: ZZ32)
  coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(small(v))
end

object Cell[\T\](c: T) end
kind(c: Cell[\ZZ32\]): String = "Cell ZZ32"
kind(c: Any): String = "other"

run(): () = do
  c: CC64 = 3 + 4 i
  assert(sEq(c.re, 3.0) AND sEq(c.im, 4.0), "3 + 4 i is CC64(3.0, 4.0)")
  d: CC64 = 3.78 + 3.243 i
  assert(sEq(d.re, 3.78) AND sEq(d.im, 3.243), "3.78 + 3.243 i is CC64(3.78, 3.243)")
  c2: CC64 = -3 - 4 i
  assert(sEq(c2.re, -3.0) AND sEq(c2.im, -4.0), "-3 - 4 i is CC64(-3.0, -4.0)")
  c3: CC64 = -3.5
  assert(sEq(c3.re, -3.5) AND sEq(c3.im, -0.0), "-3.5 at CC64 is CC64's minus on the coercion of 3.5")
  p: Dec = 3.14159
  assert(p.unscaled = 314159, "Dec(3.14159) has the unscaled value 314159")
  assert(p.scale, 5, "Dec(3.14159) has the scale 5")
  b: BF16 = 1.00390625000000000001
  assert(b.bits, 16257, "BF16(1.00390625000000000001) rounds once, to 0x3F81")
  b0: BF16 = 1.00390625
  assert(b0.bits, 16256, "BF16(1.00390625), the midpoint, rounds to even, 0x3F80")
  writtenBack(3.78, "3.78")
  writtenBack(3.0, "3.0")
  writtenBack(0.05, "0.05")
  writtenBack(1.00_16, "1.00_16")
  writtenBack(C.8_16, "C.8_16")
  writtenBack(0.1_2, "0.1_2")
  writtenBack(FF_16, "FF_16")
  writtenBack(1011_2, "1011_2")
  writtenBack(3.1415926535897932384, "3.1415926535897932384")
  writtenBack(2.500, "2.500")
  writtenBack(100, "100")
  writtenBack(0.0, "0.0")
  writtenBack(0, "0")
  writtenBack(007, "007")
  writtenBack(12_10, "12", "12_10 comes back as 12, its radix 10 lost: its four numbers are those of 12")
  writtenBack(3.5_10, "3.5", "3.5_10 comes back as 3.5, its radix 10 lost: its four numbers are those of 3.5")
  t: Tally = -3
  assert(t.k, -3, "-3 at Tally is Tally's minus on the coercion of 3")
  assert(t.seen = 3, "the coercion sees the written numeral 3")
  assert(t.negated, "Tally's own minus ran on -3")
  z: ZZ32 = -2147483648
  zz: ZZ32 = z + 2147483647
  assert(zz, -1, "-2147483648 at ZZ32 folds exactly, then converts")
  r: RR64 = -0.0
  one: RR64 = 1.0
  assert((one / r) < 0.0, "1/r is -Infinity for r: RR64 = -0.0")
  assert(sEq(site(), site()), "a numeral at a program's generic type is one object per place")
  g1: Gen[\RR64\] = 3
  g2: Gen[\RR64\] = 3
  assert(NOT sEq(g1, g2), "two places at a program's generic type give two objects")
  y: Byte = 255
  assert(y.b, 255, "255 at a byte type whose coercion holds v < 256")
  assert(sEq(0.1_2, 0.5), "0.1_2 SEQV 0.5")
  assert(NOT (0.1 = 0.1_16), "0.1 = 0.1_16 is false")
  u: NN32 = 0
  assert(u = 0, "u = 0 for u: NN32 = 0")
  x = 3
  assert(tName(x), "ZZ32", "x = 3 is a ZZ32")
  assert(kind(Cell(3)), "Cell ZZ32", "Cell(3) is a Cell of ZZ32")
  println("PASS")
end


bigToZZ64(z: ZZ): ZZ64 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.bigOverflowingToLong")
end

(* A program's coercion from the numeral type that raises fails the load of the component's class, so the program's run never starts. *)
component NumeralCoercionRaisesCompiled
export Executable

object Odd(v: ZZ32)
  coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = do
    println("coerce")
    w: ZZ32 = bigToZZ64(v).asZZ32
    Odd(w DIV 0)
  end
end

one(): Odd = 1

run(): () = do
  println("start")
  o = one()
  assert(o.v, 1, "the site's value")
end


bigToZZ64(z: ZZ): ZZ64 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.bigOverflowingToLong")
end
tests=NumeralCoercionRaisesCompiled
link
run
run_exits_nonzero=true
run_out_equals=coerce\n
run_err_contains=NumeralCoercionRaisesCompiled.<clinit>
(* The static numerals: a negative constant through the type's own minus, a generic program type, a static expression through a coercion from QQ, the defaults, and no numeral value at run time. *)
component NumeralStaticDesignWalk
import Reflect.{ typeOf }
export Executable

oneRounding(v: ZZ, r: ZZ32, m: ZZ32): RR64 =
    builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleDoubleArith.numeralToDouble")

value object CC64(re: RR64, im: RR64)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = CC64(oneRounding(v, r.asZZ32, 0), 0.0)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) =
        CC64(oneRounding(v, r.asZZ32, m.asZZ32), 0.0)
    opr -(self): CC64 = CC64(-re, -im)
    opr +(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re + other.re, im + other.im)
    opr -(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re - other.re, im - other.im)
    opr juxtaposition(self, other: CC64): CC64 =
        CC64(re other.re - im other.im, re other.im + im other.re)
end

i: CC64 = CC64(0.0, 1.0)

value object Tally(k: ZZ32, seen: ZZ, negated: Boolean)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = Tally(v.asZZ32, v, false)
    opr -(self): Tally = Tally(-k, seen, true)
end

object Gen[\T\](v: ZZ)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = Gen[\T\](v)
end

site(): Gen[\RR64\] = 3

value object Half(lo: QQ)
    coerce(q: QQ) = Half(q)
end

object Cell[\T\](c: T) end

value object Byte(b: ZZ32)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v.asZZ32)
end

isZZ32(a: Any): Boolean = typecase a of ZZ32 => true; else => false end
isCellZZ32(a: Any): Boolean = typecase a of Cell[\ZZ32\] => true; else => false end

run(): () = do
    t: Tally = -3
    assert(t.k, -3, "-3 at Tally is Tally's minus on the coercion of 3")
    assert(t.seen, big(3), "the coercion sees the written numeral 3, without its sign")
    assert(t.negated, "Tally's own minus ran on -3")
    c: CC64 = -3 - 4 i
    assert(c.re SEQV -3.0, "-3 - 4 i has the real part -3.0")
    assert(c.im SEQV -4.0, "-3 - 4 i has the imaginary part -4.0")
    c3: CC64 = -3.5
    assert((c3.re SEQV -3.5) AND (c3.im SEQV -0.0), "-3.5 at CC64 is CC64's minus on the coercion of 3.5")
    z: ZZ32 = -2147483648
    assert(z + 2147483647, -1, "-2147483648 at ZZ32 folds exactly, then converts")
    r: RR64 = -0.0
    assert(r.rawBits, -9223372036854775808, "-0.0 at RR64 is IEEE's negative zero")
    assert((1/r).isInfinite AND (1/r) < 0, "1/r is -Infinity for r: RR64 = -0.0")
    assert(site() SEQV site(), "a numeral at a program's generic type is one object per place")
    g1: Gen[\RR64\] = 3
    g2: Gen[\RR64\] = 3
    assert(NOT (g1 SEQV g2), "two places at a program's generic type give two objects")
    assert(g1.v, big(3), "g: Gen of RR64 = 3 sees the value 3")
    h: Half = 10/20
    assert(h.lo = 1/2, "10/20 at a type with a coercion from QQ reaches it as the QQ 1/2")
    assert(0.1_2 SEQV 0.5, "0.1_2 SEQV 0.5")
    assert(NOT (0.1 = 0.1_16), "0.1 = 0.1_16 is false")
    q: QQ = 0.1
    assert(numerator(q), big(1), "q: QQ = 0.1 is exactly 1/10")
    assert(denominator(q), big(10), "q: QQ = 0.1 is exactly 1/10")
    f: RR64 = 0.1
    assert(f.rawBits, 4591870180066957722, "f: RR64 = 0.1 rounds once")
    y: Byte = 255
    assert(y.b, 255, "255 at a byte type whose coercion holds v < 256")
    x = 3
    assert(isZZ32(x), "x = 3 is a ZZ32")
    assert(isCellZZ32(Cell(3)), "Cell(3) is a Cell of ZZ32")
    assert(typeOf(3).asString, "ZZ32", "typeOf(3) shows no numeral type")

# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## Two layers of code

The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.

The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.

The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:

- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.

An edit makes stale what was built from it:

- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
140:    bin/fortress P.fss
142:- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
144:- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
148:- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics

FACTS.md:250
- F-347 **Every numeral's place on the compiled path whose type names no type parameter is one value made before the program runs: a JVM constant where the fold of its type's own numeral coercion ends in an `int`, `long`, `float` or `double`, else a static final filled once by the coercion's method of the four numbers as `ZZ` values.** The code generator folds the body of the place's type's coercion, the library's or a program's, over a fragment of constants, bound names, natives over the built-in types' representations and calls of functions and methods in the fragment (`compiler/codegen/NumeralCoercionFold.java`); the method, `coerce_T№natural` or `coerce_T№point`, is compiled once in the declaring component and called from any component, and a program type's minus on a negative constant runs once with it (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`). A place whose type names a type parameter calls the method at each evaluation (row 957). A coercion whose body puts two calls of the program's own functions in one operator or one argument list, as `small(n) - small(m)` does, spawns a task, and the spawn fails the class's load (row 971); bind the operands to locals first. Under walk a folded constant at a library type converts from its exact value. Tests: `compiler/desugarer/NumeralCoercionFoldJUTest`, `library_tests/NumeralFoldIntegers`, `NumeralFoldFloats`, `compiler_tests/NumeralAcrossComponent`, `NumeralMinusOnceCompiled`, `NumeralCoercionOnceCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-static-numerals/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".

FACTS.md:246
- F-340 **On the compiled path a folded constant at a typed place of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` or `RR32` is that type's constant, a float rounded once from its exact value, and a numeral as written there is its type's own coercion folded (F-347).** The coercion desugarer types a folded constant, a negative one among them, at the place's type, and leaves a numeral as written its call of the type's numeral coercion (`compiler/desugarer/CoercionDesugarer.scala`); the code generator emits the type's `make` for the first, a float from `roundToDouble` or `roundToFloat` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`, `forIntLiteralExpr`, `forFloatLiteralExpr`), and folds the coercion's body for the second, so `x: RR64 = 0.9999999999999999` is below 1.0. A place whose value is no JVM constant is a static field `numeral$coercion$N` of the component's class, filled in its static initializer, and a coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A place whose type names a type parameter is not hoisted (row 957). Tests: `compiler_tests/FloatNumeralOneRounding.test`, `NumeralCoercionOnceCompiled.test`, `NumeralCoercionRaisesCompiled.test`, `library_tests/NumeralFoldFloats.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-literal-fold/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why"; `compile-ladder/rung-static-numerals/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The checker and the one library

FACTS.md:54
- F-57 **A numeral's type depends on the path and on the library in scope, and in generic code only the getters `x.zero` and `x.one` and the witness `typecase` give a `T` on both paths.** The witness `typecase` is a `typecase` over a function of type `() -> T`, with one clause for each number type (P-78). The checker types a numeral by its own numeral type, `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]`, which the compiler's prelude and the one library each declare (`compiler/Types.java`, `useCompilerLibraries` and `useFortressLibraries`; F-79), and converts it into its default where nothing fixes a type (F-342). Where nothing fixes a type, walk gives an integer numeral its default by its magnitude, a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ`, which it prints by those names; where its place fixes a type, walk converts it (F-341). In code generic over `T extends Integral[\T\]`, `x + 1` fails the checker but runs under walk: no coercion from a numeral into the type parameter `T` itself can be declared, since such a coercion is refused as a cyclic hierarchy. The checker refuses a numeral outside a bounded number type's range, or rounding to an infinity, statically, and walk refuses an integer numeral out of range when it runs, at the place it does not fit (F-342, F-341). Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage.md` section 2.3; `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md` sections 3.1, 4.1 and 6.2, measured on an earlier library (F-79); `x.zero` by reading, not measured.
